content: In several studies, it has been assumed that individuals without abnormalities on chest X-rays (CXR) and without a minimum set of symptoms are unlikely to have active tuberculosis (TB). In such cases, a positive culture may be transient, due to laboratory cross-contamination, or indicative of subclinical TB. This approach is a standard design in TB prevalence surveys. The sensitivity and specificity of abnormal CXR findings for detecting TB (sensitivity: 55%, 95% CI: 40–70; specificity: 89%, 95% CI: 87–91) were higher than those of persistent cough alone (sensitivity: 45%, 95% CI: 30–60; specificity: 84%, 95% CI: 82–84). However, there was a high risk of selection bias in these studies, as they included only children suspected of having TB based on symptoms, contact history, or known conversion to a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). When evaluating the performance of screening tools in a hypothetical population of 10,000 HIV-negative individuals with a 5% TB prevalence, the use of any TB symptoms alone would misclassify 54 TB patients as not having active TB, leading to inappropriate preventive treatment. In contrast, using any abnormal CXR findings would result in only 12 TB patients being misclassified and given preventive treatment. Combining any TB symptoms with any abnormal CXR findings would result in no TB patients being misclassified for preventive treatment. At a TB prevalence of 2%, using TB symptoms alone would require investigations of 16 additional non-TB patients for every TB case identified, while using abnormal CXR findings would require investigations of 7 additional non-TB patients. Combining symptoms with CXR findings would increase the number of non-TB patients requiring investigations to 15 for every TB case identified. The overall certainty of evidence for test accuracy was judged to be very low. The quality of evidence for any CXR abnormality was rated as low to moderate, while the evidence for any TB symptoms was rated as very low. There was no direct evidence on the combination of CXR abnormalities and TB symptoms, further lowering the overall certainty of evidence. The anticipated benefit of screening is the correct identification of individuals without active TB (true negatives), making them eligible for TB preventive treatment (TPT). However, the undesirable effect is the incorrect classification of individuals with active TB as not having TB (false negatives), leading to inappropriate preventive treatment instead of active TB treatment. Additionally, individuals with false-positive results would undergo unnecessary investigations and delays in starting TPT. A systematic review of cost-effectiveness studies for latent TB infection (LTBI) screening and treatment, conducted for previous guidelines, found that the cost of ruling out active TB in individuals eligible for TPT ranged from $28 to $188 in high-income and upper-middle-income countries. Screening and treating LTBI among contacts of active TB patients were generally cost-saving or had favorable cost-effectiveness ratios in low TB incidence countries. However, cost-effectiveness data for various screening methods or algorithms in high TB incidence settings were not available. The WHO guidelines recommend that the absence of TB symptoms and abnormal CXR findings can be used to rule out active TB among HIV-negative household contacts aged ≥5 years and other at-risk groups before initiating TPT. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. The combination of any CXR abnormality and TB symptoms was deemed reliable for excluding active TB before providing preventive treatment. The use of CXR may increase healthcare providers' confidence in ruling out active TB and reduce concerns about drug resistance development. However, it may also incur additional costs and inconvenience for patients. In settings where CXR is unavailable, screening for any TB symptoms alone offers the highest sensitivity among symptom-based screening rules and maintains a high negative predictive value in most settings. Proper follow-up and investigation of contacts with abnormal CXR findings or TB symptoms are essential, in accordance with national guidelines and sound clinical practice. Regarding the use of IGRA as an alternative to TST for identifying individuals at risk of progressing from TB infection to active disease, the WHO guidelines state that either test can be used for LTBI testing. This strong recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. The choice between TST and IGRA depends on availability, affordability, and resource constraints. Neither test can diagnose active TB disease or replace diagnostic workup for suspected active TB cases. The GDG emphasized the need to address the global shortage of TST and called for investment in research on novel LTBI tests with better predictive value.
